absent: Full panic entry and shutdown sequence, reboot versus halt decisions, timeout handling, and smp coordination beyond the routed helpers.
Definitions, types and locking of globals such as panic_timeout, panic_on_oops, panic_print, warn_limit, tainted_mask and console state.
Implementations of referenced helpers for backtraces, dumps, module listing, register display, sysctl handlers and ring buffer reservation.
Layouts of control, console, rcuwait, printk record and device info structures beyond the fields touched here.
Scheduler, interrupt and per-processor storage details underlying caller identity and emergency nesting counters.

findings.text: The taint reporting interface exposes two read-only accessors that return a shared buffer holding either a compact one-character-per-flag rendering or a verbose list of set flags with names, selected by a boolean parameter in a common helper.

The formatted kernel log path exposes a variadic entry that forwards to a default wrapper and then to an emit routine and a store routine; the store routine timestamps, identifies the caller, parses embedded level directives, handles continuation records, and commits into the ring buffer.

Oops handling exposes entry, exit and permission queries; entry raises emergency state and optionally triggers backtraces on all processors, exit balances entry, emits an end marker and invokes the oops dump hook.

Warning reporting exposes a function that emits a header with location and task identity, forwards optional formatted arguments to the log, dumps related state, evaluates escalation policy, records the taint, and balances emergency nesting.

Non-maskable-interrupt panic helpers expose a weak self-stop hook, a reset that marks no processor as panicking, an entry that starts a panic or parks the local processor if another processor already panics, and a warn escalation check.

Panic tunables are exposed through a kernel sysctl directory registered at boot, with handlers for backtrace control, taint display, timeouts, warn escalation, warn limit, overflow control where configured, and two views of the system-info bitmask.

Boot parameters allow presetting the system-info bitmask and selecting a forced panic processor with validation of the identifier range; a late boot hook allocates a fixed-size message buffer only when a forced processor was chosen.
Warning count is exposed as a read-only sysfs file under the kernel object that formats the current atomic counter as decimal text.

Each taint descriptor holds a character used when the flag is set, a character used when clear, and a name string; the table is indexed by flag number and built by a helper that stringifies the flag identifier.
Warning formatting arguments are carried as a pair of a format string pointer and a variable argument list for deferred rendering by the log path.

Compact taint rendering emits a fixed idle message when no bit is set, otherwise a fixed prefix followed by one slot per flag; verbose rendering emits only set flags as bracketed character plus name pairs separated by commas.

The taint string buffer starts as a small static boot area and is replaced at boot by a dynamically sized allocation accounting for prefix, separators, per-flag decoration, names and terminator; the active pointer and size are updated together.
Warn escalation panics immediately when the warn-escalation control is enabled; otherwise it atomically increments a global counter and panics once the count reaches a configurable non-zero limit.

Log storing defaults an unspecified level to the configured default, extracts level and continuation markers from inline prefixes, propagates device and forced-console markers, appends continuations to the prior record when possible, and otherwise reserves a fresh record with truncation fallback.

Emit suppresses all output after a global suppression flag is set and drops messages from non-panicking processors during a panic unless debugging or backtrace modes allow them; scheduler-origin messages are demoted and forced to offload.
Caller identity is the current task identifier when in task context, otherwise a reserved base plus the processor number, keeping interrupt and early contexts distinct from task identifiers.

Inline prefix scanning consumes two-character level directives repeatedly, adopting the first explicit numeric level only when the incoming level is still default, and records a continuation marker when present, returning the consumed length.
Message truncation caps text to a fraction of the total log capacity and reserves room for a truncation notice when space allows, preventing a single record from occupying the whole buffer.

Pause-on-oops uses a flag plus a countdown to serialize printing processors: the first arrival claims printing rights, one waiter performs the timed stall while others poll briefly, and completion clears the flag.

Boot-time message pacing is skipped once the system is running, when no delay is configured, or when the message would already be suppressed unless forced console is active; the enabled delay variant is compiled out on other configurations.
Oops pause serialization uses an interrupt-saving spin lock around flag and counter updates, releasing the lock during millisecond stalls and reacquiring it to recheck progress.

Emergency console nesting disables preemption, increments a global atomic counter and a per-processor nesting depth on entry, and on exit decrements both with warnings against underflow before re-enabling preemption.

Legacy console handoff first attempts an immediate acquisition and refuses to spin once panic is in progress; otherwise it claims a single waiter slot under a dedicated spin lock and waits for the owner to hand over ownership.

Non-blocking console wakeup iterates consoles under an SRCU read section, filters to non-blocking consoles, and queues wake work only for consoles with an active sleeper, skipping entirely when kthreads are not running.

Printk recursion is guarded by disabling interrupts and tracking a per-context depth counter; entry beyond the maximum restores interrupts and discards the message, while normal exit decrements then restores.

Oops entry moves from normal to emergency by entering emergency context, disabling tracing and lock debugging, applying pause coordination, and optionally firing cross-processor backtraces; exit reverses pause, marks the end, leaves emergency context and triggers dump handlers.

Warning handling proceeds through emergency entry, warning-trace suppression, header and message emission, module and register dumps, escalation check, stack or trace dumps, end marker, trace closure, taint update, and emergency exit.

Emergency exit wakes non-blocking console threads only when the last nested context leaves and the current flush mode requests offload, ensuring pending messages from other processors are flushed after emergency printing.

Emit dispatches to four flush actions derived from current console state: atomic non-blocking flush, offload wakeup, direct legacy printing under disabled preemption with spinning handoff, and deferred or daemon wakeup for offloaded legacy output.
Failure to allocate the sized taint buffer is fatal and panics during boot, since later taint formatting assumes a sufficiently large shared buffer.
Invalid forced-processor boot values produce a warning and are rejected, leaving the selection unset so no extra message buffer is allocated.
Sleeper detection for console wakeup relies on a full memory barrier pairing producer visibility with waiter preparation, so omitting the barrier can lose wakeups.
Initial boot-time taint staging capacity is 350 bytes.

Panic sysctl entries use mode 644 and fixed names including oops_all_cpu_backtrace where symmetric multiprocessing is configured, tainted, panic, panic_on_oops, panic_print, panic_on_warn, warn_limit, panic_on_stackoverflow on selected builds, and panic_sys_info.

Taint display letters in flag order are P or G, F, S, R, M, B, U, D, A, W, C, I, O, E, L, K, X, T, N, J with blank for clear except the first entry which uses G, and the table length must equal the compile-time flag count.
Default panic blink hook is a function pointer taking an integer state and returning long, with a built-in no-operation implementation returning zero.
A per-processor panic redirection helper invokes the panic entry on the target with a caller-supplied message pointer.
When non-blocking console support is compiled out, the thread-wakeup helper is an empty inline with no effects.
